name: John Healey
role: British Labour politician: MP for Wentworth and Dearne since 1997 (as Wentworth until 2010), Secretary of State for Defence 2024-26, Chancellor of the Exchequer since July 2026
summary: Healey's Commons record shows a Labour MP who backs NATO and the UK nuclear deterrent, argued for halting the right to buy and controlling rent rises as shadow Housing Secretary, and as Chancellor combined fiscal rules with state-backed investment in strategic industries and devolution of business rates.

unions-good.rationale: He said trade unions have a part to play speaking up on behalf of staff (2014), and as Chancellor funded the union learning fund to back workers (2026 Budget).

decide-locally.rationale: In his October 2026 Budget he said local leaders should not have to come cap in hand to Whitehall, called devolution new powers for the people who know their areas best, and committed to retaining 100% of business rates locally.

state-directs-investment.rationale: His Budget gave the National Wealth Fund and British Business Bank a new focus on defence, dual-use technology and sovereign capability (up to 5 billion pounds) and put 140 million pounds through a sovereign AI unit channelling government investment into strategic British AI firms.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: As Chancellor he welcomed the approval of the Jackdaw gas field as a pragmatic, common-sense decision that protects jobs and energy security, while keeping a commitment to net zero by 2050.

right-to-buy-council-homes.rationale: As shadow Housing Secretary on 9 April 2019 he set out Labour's plan to stop the haemorrhage of social rented homes by halting the right to buy; in 2015 his criticism of the housing association extension was about how it was done, not a defence of the scheme.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: As Defence Secretary he called NATO the cornerstone of UK security, the commitment to it unshakable, and put a NATO-first policy at the heart of Britain's defence plans.

collective-defense.rationale: He agreed in the Commons that article 5 of the NATO treaty is the obligation of members to defend each other, and as Defence Secretary called the commitment to the alliance unshakable.

trade-labor-env-standards.rationale: He backed the EU-US trade deal as a way to regulate global capitalism by setting standards that include employment rights (2013), and quoted Roosevelt that goods made below a decent standard should be barred from trade, asking for fair as well as free trade (2014).

regional-revenue-retention.rationale: In the Budget he committed that 100% of business rates will be retained locally by the end of the decade and that mayors will get 20% of business rates from next year and a share of income tax from 2028, so that more of what an area raises stays there.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: He holds that the UK belongs in NATO, which he calls the cornerstone of its security, so he rejects staying out of the military blocs.

open-lgbt-military-service.rationale: Moving the debate on Lord Etherton's review on 12 December 2024, he called the 1967-2000 ban on LGBT people serving in the forces a dark period and said that denying them the values they were asked to defend was profoundly wrong.

rent-control.rationale: As shadow Housing Secretary he twice called for rents to be controlled (a control on rent rises in October 2017, and capping and controlling the rise in rents in November 2017), a proposal for private renting generally rather than only shortage areas.

keep-nuclear-weapons.rationale: As Defence Secretary he said the commitment to NATO and to the nuclear deterrent is unshakeable (18 July 2024) and that the UK commits its deterrent in full to NATO (2 June 2025), in office while naming Russia the most pressing threat.

international-criminal-courts.rationale: On 22 February 2024 he set out a plan to hold Putin to account working through the G7, the UN, NATO, the International Criminal Court and a special tribunal for the crime of aggression.

notes: A first audit from his own Commons words, read from the local Hansard corpus (speeches, Westminster Hall and written answers 2003-2026; division lists since 2012). Themes searched: defence and NATO, nuclear deterrent, Ukraine, Middle East, international law and criminal courts, torture and overseas operations, Chagos, housing (right to buy, rents, council homes, leasehold), tax, minimum wage, unions, welfare, devolution, Lords, referendum and Brexit, immigration and asylum, climate, nuclear power, fracking, LGBT, abortion, assisted dying, death penalty, drugs, surveillance, free trade, aid, tax havens, Scotland. Most of his many speeches as a minister state government policy or oppose other parties without stating a position that settles a statement, so most statements stay null. The Commons division lists in the corpus (about 2,200 of his votes since 2012) were not used: the debate headings attached to each division in the parsed data do not reliably say which bill or amendment was voted on, and Labour whipping makes a vote on an amendment weak evidence on a specific statement. Speeches as Defence Secretary and Chancellor speak for the government and are taken as his own words only where he speaks in the first person. The uncertainty rule is not expected to be met.
